passages.t: ‘Come and see the works of God’, and ‘Come and listen’
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “For the choirmaster. A song. A Psalm” (verse 1). The first half calls the whole world to praise. “Make a joyful noise to God, all the earth!” (verse 1). “Come and see the works of God” (verse 5). The great example is the exodus: “He turned the sea into dry land; they passed through the waters on foot” (verse 6).

Then the people remember a hard time. “For You, O God, have tested us; You have refined us like silver” (verse 10). They say, “we went through fire and water, but You brought us into abundance” (verse 12).

Halfway through, one voice takes over. “I will enter Your house with burnt offerings; I will fulfill my vows to You” (verse 13). And he calls others to hear his story. “Come and listen, all you who fear God, and I will declare what He has done for me” (verse 16). “But God has surely heard; He has attended to the sound of my prayer” (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
Verse 6 recalls two crossings: the sea at the exodus (Exodus 14), and ‘the waters’, which in Hebrew is ‘the river’. That fits the crossing of the Jordan under Joshua, when Israel “crossed over the dry ground” (Joshua 3:17). Israel told these stories at its feasts so each generation could ‘come and see’.

Silver was refined by heating it until the waste rose to the top and could be skimmed off. The process hurt the metal, but it made it pure. The net, the burdens and men riding over their heads (verses 11 and 12) are pictures of defeat and hard labour. No event is named. Readers have suggested several, but the psalm does not say.

Vows were promises made in trouble. Here the singer pays them in public, and tells everyone why.
passages.later:
God promised through Isaiah, “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you” (Isaiah 43:2). Malachi pictures God sitting “as a refiner and purifier of silver” (Malachi 3:3).

Peter writes that trials prove faith, which is “more precious than gold, which perishes even though refined by fire” (1 Peter 1:7).
passages.hard: Verse 18 says, “If I had cherished iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened.” Does that mean God only hears people who never sin? No one could pray then. The verb means to hold on to sin and treasure it, while asking God for help. It is about refusing to turn, not about having failed. Isaiah says the same: “your iniquities have built barriers between you and your God” (Isaiah 59:2). But the way back is always open: “whoever confesses and renounces them will find mercy” (Proverbs 28:13).
passages.asks:
This psalm moves from ‘come and see’ what God did for everyone, to ‘come and listen’ to what he did for me. Both matter. Faith is a shared story and a personal one.

Is there something God has brought you through, ‘fire and water’, that someone else needs to hear about? Thanks said out loud helps others believe.
